common_name: Ireland Creek Annie Bean (Early Bush Dry Soup Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; this English-origin bush bean was carried to British Columbia in the 1920s and has been maintained at Ireland Creek Farm ever since.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep directly in the garden once soil has warmed after the last frost, spacing plants 4-6 inches apart in rows 18-24 inches apart. Ireland Creek Annie is a compact, heavy-yielding bush dry bean prized for its unusually early maturity and cool-tolerance, making it a reliable choice for short-season gardens. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before shelling; the buff-yellow to mustard-colored seeds cook down quickly to a rich, creamy texture well suited to soups and purees. Keep beds weeded and evenly moist through flowering and pod set, then withhold water as pods mature and dry for harvest.

common_name: Vaquero Bean (Black and White Appaloosa-Pattern Dry Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil after last frost; a distinctive black-and-white patterned dry bean popularized by Rancho Gordo and related to the Anasazi bean.

directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 60F, spacing plants 4-6 inches apart on a bush habit that needs no staking. Vaquero produces striking black-and-white speckled dry seeds reminiscent of an Appaloosa horse's coat, with a light, faintly earthy flavor and a texture often described as potato-like when cooked. Let pods mature and dry fully on the plant before harvesting, then shell and cure the beans in a warm, airy spot for another week or two before storing. This variety cooks into a rich, dark broth and holds its shape well through long, slow simmering, making it a favorite for chilis and pot beans.

common_name: Yellow Indian Woman Bean (Buckskin Montana Heirloom Soup Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; a fast-maturing Montana heirloom bush bean well suited to short growing seasons.

directions: Sow seeds directly 1 inch deep after danger of frost has passed, spacing bush plants 4-6 inches apart in rows. Also known as Buckskin or Buckskin Girl, Yellow Indian Woman is a Montana heirloom that reached Native American communities through European settlers and is prized for producing heavy yields of small, milky-yellow seeds in under 75 days, among the fastest-maturing dry beans available. The mild, creamy flavor resembles a pinto bean and the seeds hold their shape well in slow-cooked soups and stews, while also cooking noticeably faster than most other dry beans. Water regularly through bloom and pod fill, then let pods dry completely on the plant before shelling and storing.

common_name: Black Coco Bean (French Dwarf Dry and Shell Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil; a compact French heirloom bean that can be picked young as a snap bean or left to mature into a black dry bean.

directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed following the last frost, spacing dwarf bush plants 4-6 inches apart; no trellising is needed. Black Coco is a French heirloom valued for its versatility, with dark lilac flowers giving way to slender pods that are tender and crisp if picked young, meaty and flavorful as fresh shell beans about ten days later, and rich and nutty once fully dried. Harvest pods for shelling when seeds have filled but pods are still green, or leave plants standing until pods dry and rattle for storage as dry beans. This variety tolerates both drought and cooler conditions better than many bush beans, making it a dependable choice across a range of climates.

common_name: Swedish Brown Bean (Öland Heirloom Soup Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; a Scandinavian heirloom bush bean documented since the 1890s and traditionally grown on the island of Öland.

directions: Sow seeds directly 1 inch deep after the last frost date, spacing compact bush plants 4-6 inches apart; the low, sturdy habit needs no support. Swedish Brown, also sold as Öland Swedish Brown, is a Scandinavian heirloom dating to at least the 1890s that produces short pods holding five to seven glossy tan-brown seeds marked with a small white eye. Leave pods on the plant until they dry and rattle, then shell and store the beans, which cook to a nutty, dense texture well suited to baked bean dishes and hearty soups. The short, stocky plants tolerate cooler summers better than many bean varieties, reflecting their northern European origin.

common_name: Doe Hill Pepper (Doe Hill Golden Bell, Pre-1900 Virginia Heirloom Sweet Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55F; a pre-1900 family heirloom sweet pepper from Doe Hill in Highland County, Virginia.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost at warm soil temperatures, then transplant into the garden once nights stay reliably above 55F and space plants 18-24 inches apart. Doe Hill is a pre-1900 Appalachian family heirloom named for the small town in Highland County, Virginia, prized for its small, flattened, deeply lobed bells that mature quickly from green to bright orange. The thick flesh and sweet, multidimensional flavor are notably good for such a small fruit, and its early, dependable production makes it an excellent choice for short-season gardens. Plants are compact and disease tolerant; harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or wait for full orange color and maximum sweetness.

common_name: Beaver Dam Pepper (Wisconsin Hungarian Heirloom Mild Hot Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil warms; a Hungarian family heirloom brought to Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, in 1912 and listed in the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste.

directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant outdoors once nighttime temperatures stay above 55F, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Beaver Dam is a Hungarian-American heirloom brought to Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, by immigrant Joe Hussli in 1912 and is still celebrated there with an annual pepper festival; it is also listed in the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste. Fruits are large, horn-shaped, and mildly hot, roughly comparable to a pimento in heat, ripening from lime green to a deep reddish-orange and reaching 6-9 inches long on tall, vigorous plants. Harvest green for milder flavor or let fruits ripen fully red for sweeter, more intense flavor; plants are heavy yielding and adapt well to a range of climates.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

common_name: Sheepnose Pimento Pepper (Ohio Amish Heirloom Sweet Pimento)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of frost has passed; an Ohio Amish heirloom pimento pepper grown for its thick, sweet flesh.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into the garden after soil has warmed and space plants 18-24 inches apart. Sheepnose Pimento is a cherished Ohio Amish heirloom named for its squat, heart-shaped fruit, which ripens from green to a glossy deep red and is prized for exceptionally thick, meaty walls and an intensely sweet, almost sugary flavor. Sturdy, bushy plants are highly productive over a long season, yielding abundant fruit well suited to roasting, stuffing, canning, and fresh eating. Keep soil evenly moist and fertile through fruit set, and harvest at full red ripeness for the best flavor and thickest flesh.
